newsitem.title: UK: Leading European borrowers ready for EMU boost.
newsitem.headline: Leading European borrowers ready for EMU boost.

text.p: Bond issuer preparations for EMU are progressing smoothly as they await the broader, deeper market the euro will bring, leading borrowers told bankers at a conference on Tuesday.
The euro bond market, which will be based on credit differentiation as currency risk disappears and will be as big as the U.S. market, will also offer a greater range of products, they said.

Rene Karsenti, director general of finance at the European Investment Bank, said it would launch more "euro-tributary transactions. We have launched deals in four (EMU) currencies so far this year. There will be more."

Euro-tributary deals, or parallel bonds, or catamaran bonds, are bonds launched in more than one currency but with the same coupon and maturity date. They contain clauses which allow for their redenomination into euros after EMU.

"Issuance in prospective euro currencies is the best game in town. It sharpens name recognition (ahead of EMU)" said European Bank for Reconstruction and Development executive director Kari Nars who was, until recently, finance director at Finland's finance ministry.

The third stage of European economic and monetary union, including the introduction of the European Union's planned single currency, the euro, is prescribed by EU law to take place no later than January 1, 1999.
Bank of England executive director Ian Plenderleith, said monetary union in Europe "would be a tremendous step forward. Credit differentiation will be fundamental to the broader market."
Plenderleith said EMU would result in a restructuring of portfolios. "That is already happening...and providing the opportunity for these (euro) deals."
Britain, which is not expected to switch to the euro in 1999, has a 5.5 billion mark Eurobond maturing in October.
Christian Brand, vice-chairman at L-Bank, said it would be important for borrowers to have a liquid yield curve in euros ready for January 1999.

"We do not have a branch network ...and wanted to have direct dialogue with investors. Providing euro product at the earliest (possible) stage was important. It must help in establishing the (borrower's) name."
L-Bank launched seven-year euro-tributary bonds in French francs and marks in February, one of the first German borrowers to do so.
"There was no downside for us. The deals worked on their own. We did not (have to) leave any money on the table to make sure they worked," Brand said.
Tjeerd de Vries, a senior vice-president in Rabobank's treasury and new issues department, said opportunities for plain vanilla benchmark issuance would improve after EMU.
"But while it will be a bigger, deeper market overall some opportunity-driven deals will disappear."

Rabobank raises 10-15 billion guilders a year in a mix of institutional offerings in guilders and marks, with the balance in arbitrage-driven retail-targeted deals launched as opportunities crop up, de Vries said.

Caisse Centrale du Credit Immobilier's chief financial officer Arnaud Scuderoni said the mortgage bond sector in Europe should take off after EMU, mainly based on an expansion of Germany's Pfandbrief market.
Nobody on the panel argued against EMU starting on time. The Bank of England's Plenderleith said: "It is sensible to expect EMU to go ahead on time whatever its construction."

The costs of EMU in terms of computer systems and similar were not easy to establish, the panel said. De Vries at Rabobank said: "It is difficult to distinguish between renewal and replacement costs."
